source.title: Exploring Landscapes for Better Minima along Valleys
source.authors: Tong Zhao; Jia-Cheng Li; Yuan-Chang Zhou; Guang-Ming Tan; Wei-Le Jia

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation affecting the reported experiments.
record.tranche_reason: Reports its own comparisons of optimizer settings, batch sizes, and training outcomes against test accuracy, test perplexity, and training loss; these results bear conceptually on V4 and V5, but the adaptor is a different intervention from the named optimizer and batch-size studies.
record.gate_note: Included the paper's optimizer and batch-size results that report test performance, and its explicit discussion of training-loss and test-performance differences. Figure-only optimizer curves were not converted into numeric rows. Loss-landscape measurements such as Hessian eigenvalues and parameter drift do not measure the versioned generalization gap and are not included. Comparisons that report only training-time or memory outcomes are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons and batch-size comparisons with held-out performance. These bear on V4 and V5, although tuning is not restricted consistently and the CIFAR ResNet20 comparisons use different epoch budgets.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: the exploration adaptor, evaluated mainly as ALTO, improves performance over competing optimizers on their large-batch tasks, with a claimed average 2.5% accuracy improvement and limited small-batch gains. Their ImageNet comparison is large-batch ALTO 70.83% versus small-batch SGD 70.64%, not ALTO outperforming SGD at batch 256. These claims do not establish a generalization-gap mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: The paper introduces a gradient-based optimizer adaptor that adds an exponential moving average of gradient differences to the gradient update, and evaluates ALTO against standard optimizers. It does not reproduce the original adaptive-optimizer or large-batch interventions. It reports 3–5 times hyperparameter tuning per task, usually tuning ALTO's β1 and learning rate while tuning all hyperparameters for other optimizers.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size; dataset and task; optimizer; ALTO α and β1 settings; learning-rate tuning and schedule. Authors state larger batches generally call for larger β1 and smaller α, and small-batch gains are limited.

fits_no_version.finding: ALTO improves over Lamb and other adaptive optimizers on single-batch image, GPT-2, BERT and BiLSTM tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed optimizer can improve held-out performance over other adaptive optimizers in these settings; this alone establishes neither an adaptive-versus-SGD disadvantage nor a batch-size penalty.

fits_no_version.finding: BERT NER and text-classification fine-tuning performance varies with batch size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch-size effects also vary across NLP fine-tuning tasks; these are distinct from V5's image-classification and language-modeling tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Negative alpha produces smaller top Hessian eigenvalues, while small-batch test performance can favor positive alpha.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hessian-based flatness and optimizer performance can diverge across settings. This does not test magnitude-aware sharpness ranking generalization gaps.

record.problems: The study primarily compares optimizers rather than isolating the generalization gap. It reports test metrics but usually omits training-error values, so many rows cannot establish a training–test gap. Each result is described as a mean of three independent runs, but no error bars or significance tests are reported. ImageNet values and batch-size labels are inconsistent across the text and tables, and some flattened table layouts make optimizer-to-number mapping uncertain. Hyperparameter tuning differs: ALTO usually has only β1 and learning rate adjusted, while other optimizers have all hyperparameters tuned.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap was reached. Excluded remaining comparator rows from Table 15 (CIFAR-10 and alternate CIFAR-100 architectures), Table 9 (additional optimizer rows and metrics), Table 16 (ALTO and Lamb across further batch sizes), and Table 20 (remaining optimizer comparators), plus figure-only results in Figures 4, 5, 8–13, and 18–20. Prioritized ALTO rows and settings where outcomes differ across conditions. Hessian eigenvalue, parameter drift, parameter convergence, time, and memory results were not extracted because they do not directly measure the versioned generalization gap or claimed held-out metric.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local-connectivity explanations.

A consistently restricted learning-rate-and-schedule-only tuning protocol; equal or better adaptive training performance in the relevant SGD comparisons; controlled broader-versus-limited tuning, Adam-to-SGD switching, and word-level language-model comparisons. Adam and AdamW are included, but weight-decay coupling is not isolated.

Language-modeling batch-size sweeps; controlled tests of longer training, normalization or regularization remedies. CIFAR ResNet20 comparisons do not hold epochs fixed. Learning-rate and warmup changes are used in some experiments but not isolated as remedies.
Controlled dropout comparisons, small-training-set exceptions, and joint dropout/weight-decay removal.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, generalization-gap rankings and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing memorized versus random training examples.

missing.what: Replace R37–R46 with actual Table 4 batch-sweep results. Across 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K and 32K, ALTO accuracy is 77.22, 77.25, 77.35, 77.10, 76.87 and 76.70%; Adam is 73.08, 73.08, 73.32, 73.11, 73.09 and 72.50%; AdamW is 75.65, 74.93, 74.65, 74.40, 74.10 and 73.57%; AdaBelief is 73.32, 73.48, 73.41, 73.14, 73.00 and 72.89%. Lamb values marked with daggers are cited results and must not become this study's own result rows. Resolve the ImageNet versus ImageNet-100 naming discrepancy.

record.verdict_notes: All assessments use the supplied text. Optimizer names are training conditions, not model identities; the architecture is the model subject. Results are described as means of three runs, but uncertainty is not reported. Several rows link two versions with different directional conclusions; their single state is therefore cannot_determine, with version-specific findings stated in the problem field. CIFAR batch-size comparisons use 200 versus 400 epochs, unlike the fixed 90-epoch ImageNet comparison. Table 10 compares Adan with ALTO and does not contradict Lamb values. Results explicitly declared in rows_left_out are not listed as missing.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep past interpolation and test-error behavior.

The tested adaptive methods are compared with ALTO and other optimizers in the paper's tasks; no word-level language-model comparison is reported. Effects of broader tuning, Adam-to-SGD switching, and decoupled weight decay are not specifically tested.

Large versus small batches are compared in several image and NLP tasks, but no language-model batch-size sweep or normalization change is tested. Longer training, warmup, and learning-rate scaling are not isolated as remedies.
Dropout effects and removing dropout together with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting change in test accuracy.
